Causal analysis in R: the written tutorial

This file holds the explanation that goes with 02_causal_analysis_tutorial.R. The script holds the code and short operational comments. This file holds the reasoning, the function-by-function reference and how to read each output. Read a section here, then run the matching section of the script.

README.md is the repository overview and the file list. This is the teaching text.

What this tutorial is for

This tutorial will guide you through how to conduct a causal analysis: the first step is to draw a diagram called a DAG, of what variables you believe causes the outcome, then you use it to choose the covariates for each model to estimate total and direct effects. Models are fit with the brms package, using the outputs you can simulate what would happen if a practice changed, and test how far the assumptions could be wrong before the “causal” conclusion breaks.

The worked example provided here is a simulated RVFV serosurvey in cattle. The data structure is based on the real study but the premise, variables and serodata are fake. The analysis follows the analysis structure of Lim et al. (2026), Local habitual movement as a mechanism for Schistosoma mansoni transmission resurgence: a causal analysis of cross-sectional survey data, BMJ Public Health 4:e004500, doi:10.1136/bmjph-2025-004500.

Why standard regression is not sufficient: a worked example

But why use a causal analysis and not just standard regression?

Say you want to know whether grazing style has an impact on sero-status. Your most basic model would be sero-status ~ grazing, which estimates how much serostatus differs between grazing systems and how far that difference would move in another sample from the same population. What it does not say is whether grazing causes the difference or is correlated with something else that does.

Whilst wetland-grazed cattle in this simulated survey are more often seropositive than tethered cattle, these two groups differ in more than how they are grazed. They differ in where they live, because whether an animal is wetland-grazed is decided by whether its village has wetland, and that is also where the vectors breed. They also differ in age, because farmers tether the youngest animals near the homestead, so the tethered group holds a far larger share of calves, and a calf has had fewer years in which to be infected than an adult whatever its management. In this simple model the regression coefficient grazing adds these differences together and reports the sum as one number. More data does not fix this, because a larger sample narrows the interval around the same wrong number.

The obvious response is to put the other variables into the model, which works for some of them but does not really get to your question with other variabels.

For example;

  • village and age_class are reasons the two groups of animals differ before any grazing happens (as in you live in a wetland village and so you choose wetland grazing), so including them in a regression model removes a difference that was never caused by grazing. They belong in the model and are called confounders.

  • hours_at_water is a mediator. When a style of grazing is chosen, this inherently changes the amount of time an animal will spend drinking at a waters edge, so a wetland-grazed animal will spend longer there whilst a tethered animal is more likely to have water brought to it. Including it takes out part of the effect of grazing you are trying to measure.

The two variables need opposite treatment but look identical to the model, because each enters as a column of numbers and each moves the coefficient. They also look identical in the data, since both are correlated with grazing and with seropositivity, so no correlation matrix distinguishes them. Correlation carries no direction either. Grazing and seropositivity are correlated by the same amount whether wetland grazing causes infection or farmers move sickened animals off the wetland, so the number cannot tell you which of the two is happening. This is where casual modelling comes in.

What separates them is knowledge of the biology, and a DAG is how that knowledge gets written down in a form an algorithm can read. None of this proves the structure, because the arrow direction (described below) leaves no trace in an association, so the diagram is an assumption you supply from biology and the literature. Putting it on the page is what lets a reader reject one arrow and work out what it changes.

This will hopefully make a bit more sense as you start making your DAG and going the analysis.

The research question

Does the way cattle are grazed and watered cause RVFV seropositivity, and by how much would seroprevalence fall if those practices changed?

How to use the files

Run 02_causal_analysis_tutorial.R top to bottom, one block at a time, with the matching section of this file open beside it. Every model is fitted in brms so the first run compiles around a dozen Stan programs and takes 10 to 20 minutes. After that the fits are cached in models/ and re-runs are instant. Delete models/ if you change the data or a model formula.

brms needs a working C++ toolchain, which is a program outside R rather than an R package. On macOS install the Xcode command line tools with xcode-select --install, or get Xcode from the App Store.

0. Setup

Six packages are installed and four are loaded. These will load when you run your scipt.

Package What it is for
dagitty Build the DAG, find adjustment sets, test the DAG against the data
ggdag Draw the DAG as a ggplot2 figure
tidyverse ggplot2 for every figure, dplyr for mutate() and bind_rows()
brms Fit every model
fastDummies Used inside dagitty, never called by you
CCP Used inside dagitty, never called by you

tidyverse prints a list of name conflicts when it loads, which is expected and can be ignored. The two relevant here are dplyr::filter and dplyr::lag, which mask the base versions.

fastDummies and CCP get installed but never loaded, because localTests(type = "cis.pillai") calls them internally in section 5 and stops with an error if they are missing. Installing a package puts it on your computer; loading it with library() puts its functions on your search path. A package another package calls internally needs only the first.

dir.create("figures") and dir.create("models") make the two output folders. showWarnings = FALSE stops R complaining when the folder is already there. set.seed(1) fixes the random number stream so the same run gives the same numbers twice.

1. Read the data and set reference levels

The dataset is a simulated single cross-sectional survey: 2220 cattle from 200 herds in 38 villages, with one blood sample per animal and the management of each animal recorded from its owner’s questionnaire.

Column What it is
seropositive 1 if antibodies to natural RVFV infection detected
grazing How the animal is grazed
water_source Where its drinking water comes from
hours_at_water Hours per day in or at the edge of surface water
wildlife_contact Shares grazing or watering points with wildlife
introduced_recently Bought into the herd in the last 12 months
abortion_reported Abortion or stillbirth recorded for this animal
village, age_class, sex, herd_size, herd_id Design and demography

Every management variable varies within a herd, because an owner tethers the youngest animals at the homestead while the rest of the herd goes out, and 197 of the 200 herds hold two or more grazing systems as a result. The effect of grazing can therefore be estimated separately from differences between herds.

Because this is a single visit with one blood sample per animal, the outcome is seroprevalence, the proportion carrying antibodies from any past infection, not seroconversion. Antibodies to RVFV persist for years, so an animal’s serostatus accumulates exposure over its whole life. That is why age_class has to be in the model: an adult has had more years in which to be infected than a calf, whatever its management.

Reference levels. R orders factor levels alphabetically, so the reference category in every model would be whichever level happens to come first in the alphabet. In this instance, I have decided we are testing all grazing methods against tethering at the homestead, and so the factors need to be relevled. You can set the reference to the lowest-risk or baseline level yourself with relevel(), otherwise every coefficient is a contrast against something arbitrary (i.e. just the factor which comes first in the alphabet). age_class is set with factor(levels = c(...)) instead, which fixes the whole ordering rather than only the first level.

Describe the data before modelling it. Before you do any modelling you want to have a look at the data and check it looks as it should. All your serostatus values are 0/1 for example, that none of your village have N = 0 etc. This script prints overall seroprevalence, the spread between villages, seroprevalence by grazing system, seroprevalence by age class, and a cross-tabulation of grazing against water source.

tapply(cattle$seropositive, cattle$village, mean) splits the 0/1 outcome by village and takes the mean of each group, which for a 0/1 variable is the proportion positive. 38 villages is too many to read one by one, so summary() reduces them to quantiles and sort()[c(1, 38)] picks out the lowest and the highest.

How to read it. Seroprevalence is about 36% overall, with a village median of 26% and a range from 2% to 79%, so village is a large source of variation and will have to be dealt with. Seroprevalence rises from about 14% in tethered cattle to about 69% in wetland grazers, and from 20% in calves to 42% in adults, which is expected for a cumulative marker of past exposure. Nearly three quarters of wetland grazers drink from a river or a dam, whilst over half of tethered cattle have water carried to them. Exposures that are strongly correlated like this cannot be separated by the data alone, which is the first reason you need a causal diagram rather than a regression.

2. How every model in this tutorial is fitted

The models are fitted in a Bayesian framework using brms. A Bayesian fit returns a full posterior distribution for each effect/ coefficient rather than a point estimate and an interval. This means you can say how probable an effect of a given size is. because the proprtion of values that are >0 is the probability that the value will always be that effect. The posterior draws are also then used in the counterfactual simulations in section 12.

Priors

A prior says what effect sizes are plausible before seeing the data. normal(0, 1.5) on the log-odds scale is centred on no effect and treats odds ratios beyond about 1/20 to 20 as unlikely. That is weakly informative: it rules out absurd values and leaves the data to decide everything else. Refit under a couple of other priors and report that the conclusions did not change. Priors do feel a bit hand-wavey if you have never used them before, but they also do make use of your knowledge. We can work on these together more if you are unsure.

# Lets set some binary priors for use in all our models in this tutorial

pr_bin <- c(prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "b"),
            prior(normal(0, 2),   class = "Intercept"))

class = "b" applies the prior to every regression coefficient (beta) at once and class = "Intercept" to the intercept, which needs a wider prior because it carries the population-level average seroprevalence rather than a contrast. prior() comes from brms, so library(brms) has to have run before this line or R reports could not find function "prior".

The three helper functions are described in the function reference: fit_bin() wraps the sampler settings, or_table() turns log-odds into odds ratios, and p_positive() gives the posterior probability that an effect is positive.

On that last one, the proportion of the posterior above 0 is the probability that the effect is above 0, which is a statement no frequentist model can make, because a p-value is the probability of the observed data under the null hypothesis rather than the probability of a hypothesis. The posterior probability is a property of the Bayesian framework, not of the causal analysis. The causal part is which variables went into the model.

3. The crude model: a grazing-only regression

The first model includes grazing as an explanatory variable and nothing else, so that every later model can be read as a change from this starting point.

How to read it. Wetland grazing comes out at 13.6 times the odds of seropositivity compared with tethered cattle, with a credible interval of 10.1 to 18.3, well clear of 1. The interval rules out chance as an explanation. It does not establish that grazing is the explanation, because the model contains no way to distinguish the effect of grazing from the effect of anything correlated with it.

The estimate is therefore not wrong as a description of these cattle. It is insufficient as an estimate of what grazing does, which is the quantity the research question asks for.

Sections 4 to 7 work out which variables have to enter the model to recover the effect of grazing.

4. Draw the DAG

A DAG (directed acyclic graph) is a drawing of what you believe causes what. Three rules:

  1. One node per variable.
  2. One arrow per direct cause, pointing from cause to effect.
  3. No loops. If A causes B, nothing downstream of B can cause A.

The arrows come from subject knowledge, published studies and expert opinion, never from the data. Missing an arrow that really exists is an assumption that can bias your estimate, so it is safer to include a plausible arrow than to leave it out.

The arrows in this DAG are drawn from the RVF literature: wetland and riverine grazing and shared watering points raise exposure to Aedes and Culex vectors; animals bought in to replenish a herd can import infection; shared grazing with wildlife raises vector contact.

The data in this tutorial are simulated, so the DAG matches the rules that generated them, and some of those rules are simpler than a real herd. In the simulation the chance that an animal was bought in depends on its village and its herd and on nothing about the animal, so introduced_recently has an arrow from village and none from age_class or sex. A DAG for a real dataset would be expected to have both of those arrows, because bought-in animals are mostly adults rather than calves born in the herd, and because owners buy females and males for different purposes.

The syntax

rvf_dag <- dagitty('dag {
  village                [pos="0.0,1.0"]
  grazing                [exposure, pos="1.6,2.0"]
  seropositive           [outcome, pos="5.8,2.3"]

  village -> grazing
  village -> seropositive
  grazing -> seropositive
}')

The whole DAG is one character string, wrapped in dag { ... } and passed to dagitty(). Three kinds of line go inside it.

  • A -> B means A causes B.
  • A [attribute] sets an attribute of node A. Several attributes are separated by commas inside one pair of brackets.
  • A node name on its own introduces a variable with no attributes, which is rarely needed because any name used in an arrow is created automatically.

Names must match the column names in your data exactly, otherwise the DAG cannot be tested against the data later.

Deciding the role of a node

The brackets hold two different things: a role, which changes the analysis, and a position, which changes only the figure.

Attribute What it does
[exposure] Marks the variable whose causal effect you want to estimate
[outcome] Marks the variable you are explaining
[latent] Marks a variable you believe exists but did not measure
[adjusted] Marks a variable you have already conditioned on
no attribute An ordinary measured variable

Only one role decision is a judgement call about the science, which is which variable is the exposure. It is the variable in your research question, so for “does grazing cause infection” the exposure is grazing and the outcome is seropositive. One DAG answers one such question at a time. To ask what water source does instead, pass exposure = "water_source" to adjustmentSets() rather than editing the DAG, which is what section 7 does for each of the six exposures in turn.

Confounder, mediator and collider are not attributes you set. They are roles the arrows give a node relative to the exposure and outcome you picked, and dagitty works them out from the structure.

Every connection between exposure and outcome runs along a path. Some paths carry the causal effect you want. Others carry bias. The job is to block the bias paths and leave the causal paths alone. A node’s role is the shape of the path it sits on, and there are three shapes.

Chain. grazing -> hours_at_water -> seropositive. The middle variable is a mediator, because it sits on an arrow chain from grazing to seropositive. Conditioning on it removes part of the effect you are trying to measure, so leave it out when you want the total effect.

Fork. grazing <- village -> seropositive. The middle variable is a confounder, because it has an arrow into both grazing and seropositive. It creates association without causation, so conditioning on it is required.

Collider. grazing -> abortion_reported <- seropositive. Arrows from grazing and from seropositive both point into abortion_reported, which makes it a collider. These variables are already independent through this path, and conditioning on the collider creates a false association. Never condition on it.

The same variable can change role when you change the exposure: water_source is a mediator of the grazing effect and a confounder of the hours_at_water effect. Section 6 lists the paths in this DAG and section 7 reads the adjustment sets off them.

[latent] is the one role that changes what dagitty will allow itself to use. A latent node can be drawn and reasoned about, yet it is excluded from every adjustment set, because you cannot condition on a column you do not have. Section 13 uses this to show that once distance to water is added as a latent confounder, adjustmentSets() returns nothing at all.

Deciding the position of a node

pos="0.0,1.0" gives the node’s x and y coordinates in the drawing. The two numbers are in arbitrary units, so only their relative values affect the drawing, and pos="0,1" and pos="0,100" differ only in the scale of the whole figure. The first number is the horizontal position and the second is the vertical position, so a larger first number moves the node to the right and a larger second number moves it up.

Position changes nothing about the analysis. The implied conditional independencies, the paths, the adjustment sets and every estimate are identical whether you set positions or leave them out. They exist so that the figure is readable, and a readable figure is what a reviewer uses to check your arrows.

Leave pos out and tidy_dagitty() picks a layout for you with its layout = "nicely" default, which gives a different arrangement each time unless you set a seed. For a DAG you are publishing, set the positions by hand.

The layout used here puts causal order on the horizontal axis and keeps variables of the same kind in a vertical column.

x What sits there
0.0 village, age_class, sex: the confounders, upstream of everything
1.6 grazing, the exposure, and introduced_recently
3.1 water_source and wildlife_contact
4.4 hours_at_water, downstream of both grazing and water source
5.8 seropositive, the outcome
7.2 abortion_reported, a consequence of the outcome

Reading left to right therefore follows the causal order, and the y values spread the nodes within a column so their labels do not overlap. One practical rule for choosing them: give any node whose arrow would otherwise cross several others a y value that moves it clear of them.

Drawing it

tidy_dagitty() turns the DAG into a data frame of nodes and edges, which is what ggplot2 needs. node_status() adds a column flagging which node is the exposure and which is the outcome, so the plot can colour them. The mutate() line turns the NA status of every other node into the string "other", because scale_colour_manual() needs a value to match. Labels go beside the points with nudge_y rather than inside them, because variable names are too long to fit in a circle.

The hypothesised causal structure for RVFV seropositivity in cattle, with the exposure in red and the outcome in blue

Figure 1. The DAG, written to figures/01_dag.png. Arrows point from cause to effect.

How to read it. Read the drawing and check each arrow against what you know about the system. Four features of this DAG decide everything that follows.

  • village, age_class and sex sit upstream of both grazing and seropositive, which makes them confounders of the grazing effect.
  • water_source, hours_at_water and wildlife_contact sit between grazing and seropositive, which makes them mediators. They are part of how grazing causes infection, not a nuisance to be removed.
  • abortion_reported sits downstream of seropositive, because infection causes abortion rather than the reverse.
  • hours_at_water has no arrow into grazing, because the amount of time an animal spends at water is a consequence of how it is grazed and watered.

What the arrow directions assume

The direction of every arrow is an assumption about temporal order. Two DAGs that differ only in the direction of one arrow can imply exactly the same independencies, so section 5 will accept both. The assumption has to be defended from the design and the biology: management practice is recorded for a period that precedes the blood sample, antibodies persist for years so they cannot have caused a grazing decision taken earlier, and infection precedes the abortion it causes. Where reverse causation is plausible, say so. Farmers moving sickened animals off the wetland would produce the same association as wetland grazing causing infection, and this analysis cannot tell the two apart.

5. Test the DAG against the data

A DAG makes checkable claims. Every pair of variables with no arrow between them should be independent once you condition on the right other variables. These claims are the implied conditional independencies, and impliedConditionalIndependencies() lists them. The printed form A _||_ B | C reads “A is independent of B given C”.

localTests() checks each claim in the data. type = "cis.pillai" is the version that copes with a mix of categorical and continuous variables. The dag_vars line keeps only the DAG variables that are columns in the data, because localTests() stops if a name is missing.

How to read it. estimate is the leftover association after conditioning, on a scale where 0 means the claim holds. None of the 29 tests reaches p < 0.05, where 1 or 2 would be expected from chance at the 5% level, and no estimate is above 0.15, so the DAG is compatible with the data.

The estimate comes out larger by chance alone when one of the variables has many categories, as village does with 38. For any test involving village, judge the claim by its p-value and not by the size of its estimate.

A violation that is both large and significant means an arrow you left out probably belongs in. Add it, re-test, and say in your methods that you did.

What this test cannot do is confirm the DAG, because several different DAGs imply exactly the same independencies. It only rules out DAGs that the data clearly contradict. Arrow direction is the main thing it cannot see, as set out at the end of section 4.

6. Paths

paths() lists every path between the exposure and the outcome. The three path shapes, and what to do with each, are set out in section 4 under “Deciding the role of a node”.

Confounders are found by looking for open backdoor paths, which are paths that leave the exposure through an arrow pointing into it. The grepl("^grazing <-", ...) line picks those out of the full path list by matching the arrow direction in the printed path.

How to read it. 24 paths connect grazing to seropositivity and 7 of them are backdoor paths. Every one of those 7 starts at village, age_class or sex, because those are the only three variables with an arrow into grazing. All 7 are open, and all 7 have to be blocked. You do not have to work out how by hand, because the next section does it for you. The principle is that paths leaving grazing through a backward arrow carry bias, and paths leaving through a forward arrow carry the effect.

7. Let the DAG choose your covariates

This is the step that makes the analysis causal, because adjustmentSets() reads the DAG and returns the covariates that block every bias path while leaving the causal paths intact. You no longer choose covariates by p-value, by stepwise selection or by what was in the last paper, all of which can introduce bias of their own.

effect = "total" asks for everything the exposure does to the outcome by any route. effect = "direct" asks what is left when the mediators are held fixed. The function can return more than one valid set, in which case any of them identifies the effect and you pick on grounds of measurement quality and sample size.

How to read it. The total effect of grazing needs {village, age_class, sex} and nothing else. The direct effect needs those three plus all three mediators. Each of the other exposures gets its own set, and they are not the same as each other: hours at water needs {grazing, water_source}, wildlife contact needs {grazing, village}, and recent introductions need {village} alone. One model containing every variable at once would answer none of these questions correctly, because the mediators belong in some sets and not others. In causal analysis you fit one model per exposure, not one model per analysis.

Record these sets in your methods. They are the formal statement of what your estimates mean.

8. Estimating the total effect

The outcome is binary, so the model is Bernoulli with a logit link. It contains the exposure plus the adjustment set from section 7, and nothing more.

Check convergence before reading any result. Rhat compares variation between chains with variation within them, and values above 1.01 mean the chains have not settled on the same answer and the numbers cannot be trusted. Bulk_ESS and Tail_ESS are effective sample sizes, and anything above a few hundred is fine.

The posterior predictive check simulates new datasets from the fitted model and compares them with the data you actually have. The outcome is 0/1, so type = "bars" is the right display: the pale bars are the observed counts of 0 and 1, and the dark points with intervals are what the model predicts. The default density overlay is designed for continuous outcomes and is unreadable here.

Posterior predictive check: observed counts of seronegative and seropositive animals as bars, with the model’s predicted counts and intervals as points

Figure 2. The posterior predictive check for the total-effect model, written to figures/02_ppcheck.png.

How to read it. Rhat is 1.00 and the smallest effective sample size is about 1700, well above the few hundred you need, so the chains converged. The village coefficients fill most of the printout and have the lowest effective sample sizes among the slopes, because the smallest village contributes 36 animals; scroll past them to the grazing rows. In the predictive check the observed counts sit inside the predicted range, so the model reproduces the observed seroprevalence.

Posterior intervals on the log-odds scale for communal grazing, fenced paddock and wetland grazing against tethered cattle, with a dashed line at zero

Figure 3. The total effect of each grazing system against tethered cattle, on the log-odds scale, written to figures/03_posterior_grazing.png. The thick bar is the 66% credible interval, the thin bar the 95% interval, and the dashed line at 0 is no effect.

Read each odds ratio as: the odds of being seropositive for an animal under this grazing system, divided by the odds for a tethered animal of the same age and sex in the same village. Wetland grazing comes out at OR 7.5 with a credible interval of 5.4 to 10.6, well clear of 1, so wetland grazing causes a large increase in infection risk under this DAG. Communal grazing is OR 3.2. Fenced paddock is OR 1.9 with an interval of 1.4 to 2.7, a smaller effect whose interval is also above 1.

The posterior probabilities say the same thing more directly. All three grazing systems increase risk relative to tethering with probability 1.00, because no posterior draw for any of the three coefficients is below zero.

Compare with the crude OR of 13.6 in section 3. Close to half of the crude association was village and age confounding.

9. Estimating the direct effect and reading the mediation

The direct-effect model adds the three mediators to the same adjustment set. merge() puts the two sets of odds ratios side by side on the term column, with suffixes naming which is which.

How to read it. The wetland grazing OR falls from 7.5 (total) to 3.3 (direct), and its interval drops from 5.4–10.6 to 2.3–4.9. That drop is the answer to a scientific question rather than a problem with the model. It says most of what wetland grazing does to infection risk runs through the mediators: through drinking from rivers and dams, through hours spent at the water’s edge, and through wildlife contact. This is partial mediation.

Note what this means for control. If you could keep cattle in wetland areas but change their watering and their contact with wildlife, you would remove most of the risk. The wetland location itself is doing comparatively little.

When you report the two, call the total effect “the effect of grazing”. Report the direct effect next to it, named as the direct effect and with the mediators it excludes listed. For example:

Wetland grazing increased the odds of seropositivity relative to tethering, with a total effect of OR 7.5 (95% CrI 5.4–10.6). The direct effect, which is the effect not operating through water source, hours at water or wildlife contact, was OR 3.3 (2.3–4.9).

10. Alternative model specifications

This section fits the same outcome five times, changing only which other variables go in the model alongside grazing, and compares the wetland odds ratio from each. The first three models were fitted in sections 3, 8 and 9.

Model contains Wetland OR What the number is
grazing alone 13.6 Too high. Village and age differences are counted as grazing.
grazing + village, age, sex 7.5 The total effect of grazing. This answers “what does grazing do to infection risk”.
the above + water source, hours at water, wildlife contact 3.3 The direct effect, which is the part of the grazing effect that does not go through those three.
every variable in the dataset 2.1 Not a causal estimate. It contains the three mediators and abortion together, so it matches neither the total nor the direct effect.
grazing + village, age, sex + abortion 4.9 Not a causal estimate. Abortion is a result of infection, and adding it distorts the estimate.

Adding more variables does not make an estimate safer. Two of the five models give a causal estimate because the DAG chose their variables, and the other three do not because of what was left out or added.

simulation_truth.csv holds the coefficients that generated the data, so the direct effect can be checked. The true simulated direct effect is OR 2.59. The DAG direct estimate is 3.3 with an interval of 2.3 to 4.9, so the interval contains the truth and the estimate sits above it. That is the direction in which the unmeasured confounder described in section 13 pushes it.

11. A continuous exposure: hours at surface water

The adjustment set for hours_at_water from section 7 is {grazing, water_source}, which differs from the grazing set because the backdoor paths are different.

A per-hour OR is hard to interpret, so convert it to the contrasts people care about. An odds ratio for a continuous predictor is multiplicative per unit, so the effect of k units is exp(beta * k) rather than k times the OR.

How to read it. Each extra hour per day at surface water multiplies the odds of seropositivity by 1.25, with a credible interval of 1.13 to 1.38. A small per-unit effect accumulates: four hours a day, which nearly a quarter of the wetland-grazed cattle exceed, carries about 2.4 times the odds of an animal with no surface-water contact. Report the cumulative contrast as well as the coefficient.

This estimate assumes the effect is linear on the log-odds scale. Check that before trusting it, for instance by refitting with s() splines or with hours cut into bands, and say what you found.

12. Counterfactual interventions

A coefficient answers “how much more likely is infection in wetland-grazed cattle”. A counterfactual answers “what would seroprevalence be if those cattle were grazed differently”. The second is the question a control programme actually asks.

The recipe:

  1. Copy the observed data.
  2. Edit the exposure column to the intervened value, plus any variable downstream of it that must change as a consequence.
  3. Predict from the model that was fitted to the original data.
  4. Compare predictions on the original and edited data, draw by draw.

Step 3 is important because refitting the model to the edited data would answer a different question. The fitted model is the causal mechanism and the edited data is the new input.

Step 4 is important because the difference has to be computed inside each posterior draw and then summarised. Subtracting two summary means gives a number with no interval attached, whereas differencing draw by draw gives a posterior for the reduction itself.

Scenario A: move all wetland grazers to tethered grazing

How to read it. Seroprevalence in the whole population falls from 36% to 29%, a drop of about 7 percentage points. Among the wetland-grazed animals themselves it falls from 69% to 30%, a drop of about 39 points. That gap shows that an intervention can work well for the individuals it reaches and still move the population number only a little, because those individuals are a minority of the herd. Report both numbers. The subgroup figure is what a farmer experiences and the population figure is what a control programme achieves.

Taking the difference draw by draw gives an interval on the reduction itself. Here it runs from 5.9 to 8.1 points and stays clear of zero, so the reduction is supported.

Scenario B: remove surface-water contact, do(hours_at_water = 0)

The same recipe applied to the continuous exposure, using the model from section 11.

Scenario C: intervene on grazing and its downstream consequences

When you move an animal from wetland to tethered grazing, its water source and its hours at water cannot stay as they were. Scenario A did not need to edit them, because the total-effect model deliberately contains no mediators, so the indirect routes are already inside its grazing coefficient. To edit them explicitly you need a model that contains them, which is the direct-effect model.

How to read it. Scenario A left these animals at 30% and scenario C leaves them at 21%. The two routes disagree because they are not the same intervention, which is the lesson of this block.

Scenario A moves the animals to tethered grazing and lets the model supply the average consequences of being tethered. Real tethered cattle are a mixed group: some still drink at a dam, some share watering points with wildlife, and their mean hours at water is above zero. Scenario C instead forces every mediator to its most protective value at once, so it describes a far more complete intervention than changing how an animal is grazed.

Pick the one that matches the policy you want to cost. “Move the herd off the wetland” is scenario A. “Move the herd off the wetland, carry water to it and keep it away from wildlife” is scenario C. State in your methods which mediators you intervened on, because the number depends entirely on that list.

Scenario D: does the benefit differ by grazing system?

This is a conditional average treatment effect. One average effect can hide a large effect in one subgroup and none in another.

Percentage points of seroprevalence avoided by removing surface-water contact, shown as a median and 95% credible interval for each grazing system

Figure 4. The effect of removing surface-water contact, by grazing system, written to figures/04_cate.png. Animals with some contact only.

How to read it. The reduction is about 13 percentage points for wetland grazers and 10 for communal grazers, against about 4 for fenced paddock and 2 for tethered cattle, who had little contact to remove in the first place. A programme that provided troughs to every herd would spend most of its budget on the last two groups for almost no return. Targeting wetland and communal herds captures nearly all of the benefit. A single average effect would have hidden that completely.

13. Sensitivity analysis: how wrong could this be?

Every causal estimate rests on assumptions. Sensitivity analysis asks how far off the assumptions would have to be to overturn the conclusion. Three checks cover most of what reviewers ask.

(a) Unmeasured confounding: the E-value

The E-value is the minimum strength of association, on the risk-ratio scale, that an unmeasured confounder would need with both the exposure and the outcome to explain away the observed effect. A large E-value means a strong hidden confounder would be needed, so the finding is robust.

How to read it. An E-value of 7.4 for the point estimate means a hidden confounder would need a seven-fold association with both wetland grazing and seropositivity, over and above village, age and sex, to reduce the effect to nothing. Few plausible confounders are that strong, so the finding is robust. The E-value for the lower credible limit is 6.2 and answers the more demanding question of what it would take to push the whole interval across 1. For comparison, the highest-risk village in this dataset has an OR of 7.4 against the reference village, so an association of this strength does occur here. Village is the one thing you did measure that is as strong as the E-value demands, which is why it is in the adjustment set.

What is actually hidden here. The simulation that made these data contains one variable that is not in the CSV: distance from the homestead to standing water. It affects both grazing system and infection, so it is a genuine unmeasured confounder. It pushes the direct-effect estimate in section 10 above the simulated truth, and nothing in the data shows that it is there. Real surveys always have at least one of these. Say what you think yours is.

The DAG you can draw and the DAG you believe are not the same thing. Marking the hidden variable as [latent] and asking adjustmentSets() again returns an empty result, which means no set of measured variables identifies the effect. The honest conclusion is that the estimate is conditional on the unmeasured confounder being weak, and the E-value quantifies how weak.

(b) What if a mediator is really a confounder?

The DAG puts water_source, hours_at_water and wildlife_contact between grazing and infection. If any of them is in fact a common cause, it belongs in the adjustment set. You cannot settle this from the data, so show your estimate under every combination and let the reader judge. expand.grid() builds the eight on/off combinations and reformulate() turns each one into a model formula.

How to read it. The OR ranges from 3.3 to 7.5 across the eight models. Every interval stays above 1, so the direction of the finding survives whichever structural assumption you make, and that is the headline of this table. The magnitude does not survive: conditioning on water source brings the estimate to 4.9 and conditioning on hours at water brings it to 3.6, as partial mediation predicts, while conditioning on wildlife contact alone moves it from 7.5 to 7.1.

Report the whole table rather than the single model you prefer. It tells the reader that your headline number rests on a structural choice, shows them what that choice is, and lets them see how much it is worth.

(c) Measurement error in a self-reported exposure

hours_at_water comes from asking the farmer, and farmers under-report time at water. If they report only a fraction f of the true hours, the fitted coefficient under-states the true one by the same fraction, so dividing the coefficient by f corrects it.

How to read it. Under-reporting biases this estimate towards no effect, so the observed coefficient is a lower bound. If farmers report half the true time, the four-hour contrast rises from OR 2.4 to OR 5.9. The direction of the bias is the useful part, because it means the real effect is at least as large as reported, never smaller.

The three assumptions no test covers

Sensitivity analysis quantifies confounding and measurement error. Three assumptions underlie the whole analysis and none of them is tested anywhere in this script.

  • Temporality. Every arrow assumes the cause preceded the effect, and a cross-sectional survey measures everything at once. The defence is the design and the biology, as set out at the end of section 4.
  • Positivity. Every combination of exposure and covariate values has to occur in the data, otherwise the model extrapolates. Check the cross-tabulations from section 1 for empty cells before trusting a counterfactual that relies on them.
  • Consistency. The intervention you simulate has to correspond to a real-world action with a single meaning. “Tethered at the homestead” has to mean the same practice for every animal you move into that category.

State all three in the limitations.

14. How to write this up

Methods section, in order:

  1. The DAG, as a figure, with a sentence on where each arrow came from.
  2. That you tested the implied conditional independencies, and the result.
  3. A table of the adjustment set used for each exposure–outcome pair.
  4. The model family and link for each outcome, and the priors if Bayesian.
  5. Convergence diagnostics, Rhat and effective sample size.
  6. The sensitivity analyses, including E-values.

Results section: report total and direct effects separately and label them as such. Give counterfactual results for both the whole population and the targeted subgroup, because they answer different policy questions. Use credible intervals and posterior probabilities rather than p-values.

Say plainly what the estimates do and do not support. “Under the causal structure in figure 1, wetland grazing causes an estimated 7.5-fold increase in the odds of RVFV seropositivity” is a claim a reader can check and disagree with. “Wetland grazing was significantly associated with seropositivity” is not.

Three things to remember:

  • The DAG is an assumption, not a result. Publish it so others can argue.
  • Total and direct effects are different quantities. Never report one as the other.
  • More covariates is not more rigorous. Mediators and colliders both make estimates worse.

Function reference

Functions written in 01_simulate_data.R

inv_logit(x) turns a number on the log-odds scale into a probability between 0 and 1. The simulation builds each risk as a sum of log-odds terms, and rbinom() needs a probability, so this is the conversion between the two. inv_logit(0) is 0.5, inv_logit(2) is 0.88.

softmax_pick(scores, labels) does the same job for a variable with more than two categories. It takes a matrix with one row per animal and one column per category, exponentiates every entry so all are positive, divides each row by its total so the row sums to 1, and draws one category per row with sample.int() using those probabilities. The “score” in each cell is the sum of the simulated effects acting on that animal for that category, so a larger score makes that category more likely without forcing it.

Functions written in 02_causal_analysis_tutorial.R

fit_bin(formula, name) fits one Bernoulli logit model with the settings used everywhere in the tutorial, so the sampler arguments are written once instead of a dozen times. chains = 4 runs four independent chains, iter = 3000 with warmup = 1000 keeps 2000 draws from each, cores = 4 runs the chains in parallel, refresh = 0 suppresses the progress output, and file = writes the fit to models/<name>.rds. The file argument is what makes the second run instant: brm() loads the saved fit instead of compiling and sampling again. Delete the file, or the whole models/ folder, when you change the data or the formula, because brm() does not check whether the saved fit still matches.

or_table(fit, keep = NULL) turns the log-odds coefficients into odds ratios with their 95% credible interval. fixef(fit) returns a matrix of population-level coefficients with columns Estimate, Est.Error, Q2.5 and Q97.5, and exp() moves each to the odds-ratio scale. keep is a regular expression matched against the coefficient names, so keep = "grazing" prints the four grazing rows and leaves out the 37 village rows.

p_positive(fit, keep) gives the posterior probability that an effect is positive. as_draws_df(fit) returns one row per posterior draw and one column per parameter, and mean(x > 0) is the proportion of draws above zero. A value of 0.97 means that under this model and these data there is a 97% probability the effect raises the odds.

wetland_or(fit) pulls the wetland grazing coefficient out of any fit and exponentiates it, so the five specifications in section 10 can be lined up in one table.

pop_mean(fit, newdata, rows = NULL) returns a posterior for the population seroprevalence. posterior_epred() gives a matrix with one row per posterior draw and one column per animal, holding each animal’s predicted probability under that draw. rowMeans() averages across animals within each draw, which leaves one seroprevalence per draw, so the result is a posterior distribution rather than a single number. rows restricts the average to a subset of animals, which is how the subgroup figures in section 12 are produced.

q(x) summarises any posterior vector as a mean and a 2.5%–97.5% interval, converted to percentages and rounded. It is used on seroprevalences and on differences between them.

e_value(or, p0) computes the E-value. It first converts the odds ratio to a risk ratio using the baseline risk p0, because the E-value formula is defined on the risk-ratio scale, inverts the result if it is below 1 so the formula sees a ratio above 1, then returns rr + sqrt(rr * (rr - 1)).

Functions from dagitty

dagitty(string) parses the dag { ... } string into a DAG object.

impliedConditionalIndependencies(dag) lists every independence the structure implies. Each one is a claim the data can contradict.

localTests(dag, data, type = "cis.pillai") tests each of those claims in the data and returns an estimate, a p-value and a confidence interval per claim. cis.pillai uses the Pillai trace from canonical correlation analysis, which handles a mix of categorical and continuous variables. It calls fastDummies and CCP internally, which is why both are installed.

paths(dag, from, to) lists every path between two variables, with the arrow directions shown, in $paths.

adjustmentSets(dag, exposure, outcome, effect) returns the sets of measured variables that identify the chosen effect. An empty result means no such set exists among the variables you have.

coordinates(dag) returns the pos values as two named vectors, which is useful for checking that a node went where you meant it to.

Functions from ggdag

tidy_dagitty(dag) converts the DAG into a data frame of nodes and edges with x, y, xend and yend columns, which is the format ggplot2 needs. Without pos attributes it computes a layout, using layout = "nicely" by default.

node_status(tidy_dag) adds a status column marking the exposure and the outcome, so the plot can colour them differently.

geom_dag_edges(), geom_dag_point(), geom_dag_text() and theme_dag() are ggplot2 layers for arrows, nodes, labels and a blank background with no axes.

Functions from brms

brm() fits the model. prior() builds a prior specification. fixef() extracts population-level coefficients. as_draws_df() returns the raw posterior draws. rhat() returns the convergence statistic for every parameter. pp_check() draws the posterior predictive check. mcmc_plot() draws posterior intervals. posterior_epred() returns expected values on the response scale for new data, which is the engine of every counterfactual in section 12.

Base R functions worth knowing here

relevel(f, ref) moves one level of a factor to the front, making it the reference category. tapply(x, g, FUN) splits x by group g and applies FUN to each piece. reformulate(termlabels, response) builds a formula from character strings, which is how the eight models in section 13(b) are generated in a loop. expand.grid() builds every combination of a set of values. merge(x, y, by, suffixes) joins two data frames on a shared column.
